utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. We are now ready to commence the Defence cases in this trial. Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. The Defence of Mr. Mrksic will now give its opening statement in accordance with the Rules, while simultaneously in keeping with the recommendation of the Trial Chamber that this opening statement be brief as and succinct as possible and not resemble the closing arguments or any evaluation of evidence. The Defence of Mr. Mrksic, in the course of our Defence case by means of witnesses and other evidence, will demonstrate the role of Colonel Mrksic during the time relevant to the indictment as commander of the Motorised Brigade and commander of the Operative Group South. In addition to that, we will lead evidence which will go to show that the accused Mrksic did not participate in the joint criminal enterprise, as charged by the indictment, nor was his objective to persecute Croats and other non-Serbs who, following the fall of Vukovar, found themselves in the Vukovar Hospital by committing crimes, inhumane and cruel treatment, and similar acts against these people. When it comes to Mr. Mrksic, his Defence rejects the argument of the Prosecution, namely, that the crimes listed in charges 2 to 8 were natural and foreseeable consequences of the joint criminal enterprise, nor do we accept that he was aware that such crimes were possible consequences of joint criminal enterprise. Mile Mrksic at that time was a colonel in the Yugoslav People's Army. In 1991, he was commander of the Motorised Guards Brigade, which was an elite unit for special purposes, headquartered in Belgrade. This unit, as is true of the entire JNA, was a multinational formation in accordance with the then valid principle of brotherhood and unity. Acting pursuant to the order of the federal secretary of defence, who was his superior, Mr. Mrksic went to Negoslavci with his brigade and, once again, pursuant to the order, took over the role of commander of the Operative Group South. I believe that it is beyond dispute that this order was issued at the time when the fighting in Vukovar was well under way. Even though it was not up to Mr. Mrksic to go into analysis of what caused this conflict, the Defence believes that the Prosecution wrongly defined these military operations as occupation, whose goal it was to displace and persecute the Croatian population. Throughout our defence case, we will be leading evidence to show that in Croatia, in the course of 1991, there was an armed rebellion, first by means of illegal arming of a large number of Croats and then by creating paramilitary formations which initially intimidated the non-Croat population. When it comes to Vukovar and the surrounding area, there were almost as many non-Croats as Croats, because that area was populated by a mix of Croats, Serbs, Hungarians, Ruthenians, and others, although the Croats were the dominant group. When they moved from intimidation to physical elimination, in many cases, of civilians, first of all of the Serbian ethnicity, when they started torching and blowing up their homes, when they started persecuting these people, the then leadership of Yugoslavia believed that it was only the Yugoslav People's Army, as the sole armed force envisaged by the constitution, that was capable of disarming illegally armed paramilitary formations which, in the meantime, had taken over some parts of local authorities and had also blocked many barracks of the JNA in Croatia and specifically in Vukovar. Unfortunately, very serious armed fighting erupted in Vukovar. The paramilitary formations which blocked the entrance to the city and the JNA barracks there were quite numerous and determined to prevent the JNA in accomplishing its task of disarming them and restoring law and order in that area. The Defence will lead evidence to prove that Mile Mrksic, as commander of the Guards Motorised Brigade and Operative Group South, acted in accordance with all existing rules, and that he did not issue any orders that would target civilians or prisoners, that would expose them to persecution or murder. Even though he did not directly supervise the transfer of prisoners and their accommodation outside of Vukovar, because it was the local commanders that were in charge of that, he never accepted, nor did he ever order, that any of the prisoners be transferred to any other units, not even the Vukovar Territorial Defence or the Territorial Defence of Eastern Slavonia. This will be the focus of the Defence case. When it comes to tragic events, in the night between the 20th and 21st of November, 1991, the Defence will be adducing evidence to show that Mile Mrksic didn't issue any specific orders, especially not on that day, in relation to prisoners in Ovcara, nor did anyone ask him to issue such orders. On the 20th of November, immediately following the regular meeting with his subordinate officers, as was the daily practice, sometime after 1800 hours, Mile Mrksic set off to Belgrade in a passenger vehicle together with Defence witness Coric. Coric's driver drove the car. Mrksic arrived in Belgrade in his apartment in the evening hours, while the second major news programme of Radio-Television Serbia was broadcast. That evening, upon his arrival, his wife informed him that just prior to his arrival his sister had called. She had spent the entire time in Vukovar as a civilian and arrived in Belgrade in a convoy of refugees. She's currently residing in the village of Jajinci, near Belgrade. It was then that Mrksic called on the phone the headquarters of the Guards Motorised Brigade and issued an order to the driver who was on duty at that moment - and this is Defence witness Relic Nenad - to go to Jajinci, to his sister, and to bring her to his apartment. The witness did that and brought Mrksic's sister to the apartment. He stayed there for a brief period of time and then left. He was ordered to come on the following morning to pick up Mr. Mrksic and to take him to a reception held by the Minister of Defence, which was to take place on the 21st of November, in the morning hours. As we were able to see in the evidence admitted so far, Mr. Mrksic attended that reception. On the following day, on the 22nd of November, 1991, together with Major Tesic, he was first taken to the heliodrom, and the two of them were transported in a helicopter to Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During his stay in Belgrade ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you just try speaking into the microphone, Mr. Domazet. There seemed to be some problem at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are problems with my microphone. I hope you can hear me now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Yes, we can hear Mr. Domazet now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That critical night between the 20th and the 21st of November, during that particular time, Mr. Mrksic did not receive, nor did he receive later, any notice, any information about what was taking place; that is to say, he did not receive that information either during the time while he was in Belgrade or afterwards. Upon his return from Belgrade, he stayed in Negoslavci just two more days. And then on the 24th of November, with his brigade, he left that area and with his brigade returned to Belgrade without ever visiting Vukovar. The Defence will adduce evidence to show that allegations in count 9 of the indictment are not true, namely, those stating that Mr. Mrksic had effective control over, as they termed it, Serb forces, which guarded detainees, transferred and kept them at the Ovcara farm, and then later on mistreated and killed them. Even though Colonel Mrksic had no knowledge about the alleged agreement in Zagreb, nor was he ever informed about that, he did talk to Dr. Bosanac about the evacuation of the patients from the hospital, which, until that time, was not part of the area of responsibility of his Operations Group South. The Defence will be adducing evidence to show that it is not true that he ordered soldiers under his command, or rather permitted them, to transfer the control of the detainees at Ovcara to other Serb forces which physically committed these crimes. In addition to that, we will be proving that it is not true that he learned of the crimes committed and even took some steps to conceal these crimes. We will also be leading evidence to show that the command of the 1st Military District, which was superior to Operations Group South, was in charge of the sanitisation of the terrain, the victims and those who were killed, and that it was them who involved in that task experts and military investigative organs. We will be proving that it was not a task that Colonel Mrksic was issued with. Quite to the contrary. A special team of senior officers of the 1st Military District, officers from the security administration and the Federal Ministry of Defence from Belgrade, were following the events in Vukovar those days, especially those surrounding the detainees. The Defence wishes to show whose officers and under whose orders were at Ovcara during the critical time, the simple fact being they were certainly not there under Colonel Mrksic's orders. When speaking about the security officers of his own brigade or any of his subordinate units, the Defence will prove that this by no means meant or had to mean that, under all circumstances, they were acting on his orders or with his knowledge or approval; namely, there was another chain of communication running between these officers and the superior security bodies, whose tasks they were carrying out throughout in addition to their regular tasks with their own units. As for these special tasks that they were carrying out for the security organ, these tasks were not something that their regular superiors outside the security bodies knew or had to know about. And this applies to Colonel Mrksic as well. He did not necessarily know about the existence of any such assignments, and he was not necessarily receiving any reports that were being submitted to the security organ. The Defence will be trying to show this all the more so because it has been suggested that certain security officers, some of them so far unidentified, had been present at Ovcara and had effected what had happened on that day or perhaps even issued orders there. The Defence will try to use as few witnesses as possible for our case, as little time as possible, and we will be doing our best to expedite the trial, to the extent possible, and help bring the entire proceedings to a speedy and successful end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Domazet. Is it appropriate now to continue with your first witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have been informed that our witness, Mrs. Mrksic, arrived in The Hague a short time ago. I have also been told that she's present on the premises. I would like to ask the Trial Chamber one thing, though. I did not get a chance to see her. Her arrival itself had been expedited and she had not been foreseen as a witness for this week. If we are to continue with the following witness, that is, Mrs. Mrksic, could the Trial Chamber please grant me a somewhat longer break so that at least I get a chance to talk to her before she starts testifying this afternoon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, in the whole circumstances, we propose to adjourn now and resume at 4.00. Will that be adequate time?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will do that, and we'll resume here, then, at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mrs. Mrksic. Could I ask you please to stand and to read aloud the affirmation on the card that is given to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down. Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please stand closer to the microphone. The interpreters can't hear him. Thank you. Could counsel please stand closer to the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you hear me now, Mrs. Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: There seem to have been some problems with the microphone. I'll do my best to stand as close as I can. Can you please tell everybody your personal details, your first name, your last name, when you were born, and where.

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: My name is Djudjica Mrksic. I was born on the 24th of February, 1948, in Dreznica, Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. You are Mr. Mile Mrksic's wife, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am Mr. Mile Mrksic's wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When did you get married, and where?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: We got married on the 28th of December, 1969, in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Please tell me about your husband. Tell me about his family. Tell me what you know. Did he have any brothers or sisters? Where did he spend his childhood years? Tell us what you know about that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We're still having a great deal of trouble hearing Mr. Domazet. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: My husband was born in Croatia in a place called Vrgin Most. It's a multiethnic environment. He has a brother and three sisters.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know where he went to school? Do you know about his educational background?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: My husband completed his secondary schooling in Vukovar, which is another multiethnic environment. He graduated from the military academy in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you say the academy, you mean the military academy; right?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, the military academy.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You've mentioned several times that he was born and lived in a multiethnic environment. What about his family or your extended family? Were there any other relatives belonging to other ethnic groups, wives, husbands, that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, we do have multiethnic relatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if we could just briefly go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mrs. Mrksic, can you tell me about your own family? Mr. Mrksic and you, do you have any children?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Mrksic is the father of my three daughters.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In 1991, were your daughters living with you?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. All three of them were staying with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I would like to ask you some questions now in relation to that year. At the time your husband was, I suppose you know, occupying which post exactly in the army?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: My husband was the commander of the Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What about before he became the commander of that brigade? Had he not spent some time with the brigade previously?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, he had spent a substantial amount of time with the brigade beforehand.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Back in 1991, did you know that he went to that particular area with his unit?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know he was in the area with his unit back in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Were you in touch with him after he left for the area? Did you speak on the phone or did you perhaps meet throughout that time?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: We didn't meet in person but we did speak on the phone, except for the 20th. On the 20th he came in person.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: All right. First of all, you mentioned the phone calls. How many and when?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: He'd call once or twice a day. He mostly wanted to know about the children, how they were doing, and whether there was anything new to report in connection with the children.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You say he only came once. Had he ever, before that one single time, returned to Belgrade or to his home?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: He had never been home prior to this one single time that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mrs. Mrksic, can you tell me about this one time that he came? Had he announced his arrival, when, and how did that go? To the best of your recollection, of course.

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: My husband telephoned me in the evening hours. He told me to switch the water boiler on because he would soon be coming. He said he had some commitments the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember exactly when this was?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: This was the day before St. Arandjel's day, which would seem to imply that it was on the 20th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: One question for the benefit of the Chamber. You mentioned St. Arandjel. Can you tell us what that means in Serbia? Why is that an important day?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: That is the 21st of November. It's a very important holiday for the Serbs, a church holiday.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we please go back to the 20th. You say that sometime in the evening, Mrksic called to announce his arrival; right? Can you tell us exactly what happened that evening? Above all I mean when exactly did he arrive, and what did he do later?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: My husband arrived during the second T.V. news programme that evening. Just before he arrived, his sister Nada called --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you please not mention that?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, right. So he arrived during the second edition of T.V. news that evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. We might have to move into private session for this detail later on, but I want to ask you something about this. When you say the second T.V. News that evening, what time did that usually start?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: Normally it would start at 1930 hours and it would last for about half an hour, but it would sometimes take as long as an hour because of the various developments at the time and all the coverage of the theaters of war throughout the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. If I understand you correctly, normally it would take half an hour, but on the days in question it would normally last a great deal longer. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. Not just that one day. It was like that throughout this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You mentioned the phone call prior to his arrival. I'd like to ask you a couple of questions about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, if we could please move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mrs. Mrksic, you mentioned a bit ago that your husband was supposed to go to report, or perhaps he was supposed to go to a reception somewhere. Do you know when this was and how long he stayed in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: My husband went in the morning. After we had had coffee with his sister, he went to a reception or rather he went to work. I don't know what he did afterwards. The driver took him. He stayed until the following day, which is to say on the 22nd he went back, early in the morning, at 7 a.m., or rather he left even before 7 a.m., he left our apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know how he was supposed to go back, by what means?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. When my husband arrived on the 20th, in the evening, the first thing I asked him was how long he would stay, and he said that he would go back on the 22nd.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did he tell you on the 20th about the means of transportation?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise, I didn't answer your question. My husband arrived and I asked him how he had travelled, because he said that on the 22nd he would travel in a helicopter. And I asked him about how he had arrived, how he had travelled on his way there, and he said that he had travelled with Velimir Coric, former guards commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: All right. Do you know what means of transportation he used? Did he say anything about that?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: He arrived in a private vehicle. Coric travelled in a private car, and my husband joined him; that is to say, they travelled in Coric's private vehicle with his driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You said earlier that Coric was the former guards commander. Were you trying to say that he was the commander of that same unit before your husband, or is that perhaps some other unit?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: Velimir Coric was commander before my husband assumed that post, commander of the same guards unit. My husband took over the unit from Coric.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that your husband had told you that on the 22nd he would travel back in a helicopter. Do you know whether this actually transpired, whether he indeed returned to Negoslavci in helicopter?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: As far as I could understand, my husband called from Batajnica sometime around noon on the 22nd. I didn't quite understand whether they had set out and then they returned, because it was quite foggy. At any rate he told me, "I'm still at the airport. We're waiting for the fog to subside so that we can take off."

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Just to clarify, it is your evidence that from the moment when he left for the first time to Vukovar with his unit, that from that time on he didn't visit you until he came on that occasion that you just described; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Once he left to the front, he didn't come except for that once. And then on the second time, he came back with his unit on the 24th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm going to ask you some questions about your family life related to the period of time after this one. Were you employed during that time or up to this time? Did you have your own income?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did have my own income. I was employed, mostly full time, from the 1st of August, 1963, until June of 1996, when I retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So in June of 1996 you retired. Do you remember when your husband retired? Before you or after you?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: My husband retired several months before me, roughly after the Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So in 1996, you were retired and so was your husband, and this is what constituted the income for the family. What about your daughters? They were your dependents; correct?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: At the time our daughters were, and still are, our dependents. We provide for their living from our retirement benefits.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In 1996, was your pension sufficient to cover the expenses of your family of five members? Did you have any additional source of income?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: As this was not sufficient, all of us lived together. We had another source of income from working at the Kalinic market in Belgrade. My husband and I worked there for four and a half years, from morning till night, in all types of weather, snow, sleet, rain and wind. We were the first to arrive at the market and the last to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Mrksic. We are not going to go back to this topic. Can you tell us and the Chamber what you know about your husband? Can you tell us about his attitude towards people in general, towards his subordinates, and especially towards people of other ethnic backgrounds?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: First of all, I can tell you right away that my husband was never a nationalist. Quite the opposite. He socialised and met with his friends and colleagues of various ethnicities. He attended military school together with future officers of various ethnic backgrounds. At the time, if we walked in the street and if we came across any other JNA members, he would stop and always devote enough time to have a chat with everyone. He showed great respect for all of these people and he remains -- he continues doing that to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I've concluded my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Domazet. Mr. Borovic, are there any questions of Mrs. Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mrs. Mrksic, I have some questions for you, not too many. You're aware about the allegations against your husband and what happened at Ovcara; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: I don't know what happened at Ovcara since I was not at the front. I'm a mother, first and foremost. I worked in two shifts, and in addition to that I was a homemaker. As to the charges brought against my husband, I know about that from the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would it be right to say that you're aware that there were over 200 people murdered in Ovcara, and that your husband is accused of being involved in it? Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: I'm aware of that, and I feel deep regret about the death of these people. My husband is not involved in that. I know him well and I can tell you firmly here, under oath, that he would never allow for something like that to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When did you first hear about the killings in Ovcara? We know that they occurred in November 1991, and you knew that your husband was in the area of Vukovar at that time. So when did you first hear about the killings at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: As for the murders at Ovcara, I heard about that for the first time from the media, from daily -- from weeklies, daily -- from weekly Vreme and Nin in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And so in 1993, if we just take your evidence, you were aware about murders in Ovcara at a time when your husband was in charge of soldiers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: I can't answer that question because I don't know what their rules and regulations are, and I don't know what took place there. My husband wasn't there alone. There was an army of people there, many commanders, and I don't know who was responsible for what. It is true, though, that my husband was commander of the Operations Group South.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So you were aware in 1993 that murders had occurred in the area for Operations Group South that was controlled by your husband. You were aware of that allegation; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: The papers wrote about that. As to what extent that was true, the Court will establish that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And consequently, I would suggest it's only logical that you would have asked your husband, "Is this true? Did anything like this happen at Ovcara when you were there?"

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: I didn't put that question to my husband. When I mentioned it he felt very bad and he told me that he would have never done anything like that or permitted it, and that he didn't participate in it. I'm telling you this now absolutely sincerely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And so would it be right to say, about 1993, your husband indicated to you that he would have had nothing to do with that and he knew nothing about it? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't think that the witness said that her husband knew nothing about that. She said that he didn't participate in it, not that he knew nothing about it. In the question of my learned friend, it is implied that he knew nothing about the murders which occurred, which is something quite different from what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That is a fair statement, I think, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: With the utmost respect, all I'm trying to do is to find out when --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You might be trying to find out, but you did misstate the evidence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When did your husband then say that he would never have done anything like that or permitted it, and he didn't participate in it? Was that in 1993, when you mentioned it to him?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And was there a very general discussion with you and him, husband to wife and vice versa, of what on earth happened; how did these people get killed?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: He didn't discuss it with me. He just felt very bad about it. And he didn't speak about it at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You see, your husband has told courts, certainly a court, that he didn't know about this killing until about 1995, '96, somewhere roundabout that period. Now, can you explain that to us, how he's discussing it with you in 1993 with regard to knowledge but he's telling another court that he heard about it really much later?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we didn't introduce that piece of evidence here, and as far as I'm aware we do not have that particular statement of Mr. Mrksic which is now being put to his wife. And I don't think that she can be cross-examined on that topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Domazet, but the cross-examination is not confined to a matter that is presently in evidence, so the question can be put. Just what, if anything, Mrs. Mrksic will be able to say we will learn. Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Are you able to assist us about that?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor, I can't tell you anything about it since I didn't discuss it with my husband.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did your husband ever say to you, Well, actually, I handed them over or I authorised -- my mistake, I authorised these prisoners to be given over to a government and unfortunately they seemed to have been killed while under their control? Did he ever say that to you?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: No, he never told me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did he ever refer to Major Sljivancanin when discussing this topic, even in brief form?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: No, he never mentioned Major Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did he ever suggesting that people who were in charge of the operation had perhaps let him down in their tasks?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: No. No, he never said that. He never mentioned it or spoke about it. We didn't discuss any military issues at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, military issues I can perfectly understand and I can certainly sympathise, but here is a situation where atrocities occurred during his control. Did he ever suggest, for example, of going to the authorities and seeing if he could assist in any inquiries or investigations?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, my husband never discussed that with me - I state this with full responsibility - because I'm not competent when it comes to these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Might I ask when it was that you were asked to give evidence at this Tribunal by this legal team who represent him?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: I learned -- just a minute. Was it yesterday or perhaps two days ago? Two days ago I learned that I was supposed to be the first witness here, and today I arrived at the airport. At a quarter to two I went to the hotel and was supposed to appear here at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mrs. Mrksic you have my complete sympathy for the predicament that you find yourself, but can I ask you to recall when it was you actually spoke to the lawyers for the first time about this topic? Did they ever come and take a statement from you?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: No, I truly don't know that. They work with other things and they're probably too busy with those other things. They didn't come to see me and take a statement from me. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I may come back to certain areas like this, but I want to deal with other matters. You told us, and it may be a case of translation, that your husband telephoned you, as you believe, on the 20th, in the evening hours, and told you to switch on the boiler. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. On the 20th of November, in the evening hours - I don't know whether we already had the light on or not; I can't remember what time it was - but he told me that he was on his way and to turn the boiler on, that he would arrive that evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So he was on his way. Switch on the boiler and he would arrive. Did he give an indication of the time he would arrive?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, based on Mr. Moore's question, it would appear that he called while on route. That's not what the witness said. She said that he called, but the witness never said that he called after he had already set out. No, that's not what she said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't -- I'll ask the questions again and then we'll see if that helps in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When your husband telephoned, was it your understanding that he was still stationary at his headquarters?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I think you've told us he didn't say what time he would be there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: He didn't tell me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Bearing in mind you've told us that you were going to have supper, did you ask him what time he would arrive so that perhaps you would know?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: No. When he arrived, he was so tired he couldn't even eat. He took a shower and wanted to go to bed as quickly as possible. There was something he had to do before he could do that. He had to have a word with his sister.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So the sequence is, he phones from his headquarters, he's on his way, put the boiler on, and doesn't say the time. Now, can I just -- can I just clarify the situation that existed at that time. Vukovar had been liberated, and I think it's right to say it was on the Serbian news fairly extensively, along with other topics. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And through that evening there were a number of broadcasts on the television about the liberation of Vukovar. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When your husband arrived, you have three daughters; isn't that right? I won't give their names. I know their names, and I hope I'm right on it. But the three daughters lived with you at that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And is it your evidence that the three daughters were there that evening when your husband telephoned and arrived?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: My daughters were home when he arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Were your daughters present when he telephoned?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: I don't remember if they were or not. Normally they're each in their own rooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just see if we can work through this situation, because as a father one tends to deal with these problems. When your husband said he was coming home, presumably your daughters would have been pleased to see him and you would have told them. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: I didn't say anything. I was far too busy. I had so many commitments. I was still working at the time. I was gainfully employed, and there was so much that needed doing and I was in charge of everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: From memory, your eldest daughter was of university age at that time. I think she was 20/21; is that right? She was born, I think, in 1970. I'm doing it from memory. Can you help me?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, 1970.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Was she studying at university at that time?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: She didn't go to university. She went to a secondary school for nurses, and she's not as active as she used to be, and hasn't been since she turned 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What I wanted to know is, did she attend a course at that time that made either her stay out, or what time did she tend to come back, or did she even stay away? Do you see the difference?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: She didn't really leave home that often. She wasn't at school at the time, if that's what you mean. I don't believe that she was. It was quite late in the day, after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, your other two girls, I think one was 17, one was very young indeed. Let's deal with the 17-year-old. Was she attending school at that time?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: The younger one wasn't. The 17-year-old one was; she was attending school at the time, sometimes in the morning and sometimes in the afternoon, depending.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So can I summarise your evidence in the following way? Please tell me if I'm right or wrong. You can't remember if you told the girls their father was coming home.

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: I didn't want to put that sort of burden on their soldiers. I tried to spare them. They are all very emotional and there are all sorts of problems involved. When their father arrived, they saw him. They are quite fond of him. They are very attached to him, and I tried to spare them any emotional effort. Whenever he came, they all just rejoiced.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But, of course, he hadn't been there for a considerable time, had he? And this was the first time back. Are you saying you didn't tell them, truly?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: Truly. He had spent half his life away from home, and my daughters and I always wanted to have him back as often as possible. He would always take off for a fortnight. He was always somewhere else. He was always away from him. That's how committed he was to his job. And every time he turned up at our doorstep, we were invariably ecstatically happy to see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And so would it be right to say, then, they only became aware of your husband's arrival when he came through the door; is that correct? They had no notice of it before.

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult for me to provide a specific answer to that one because there was a mess in our house that evening. I was worried and concerned about the whole thing and about my sister due to arrive -- my husband's sister due to arrive, and I was the only one who was there to keep the whole thing under control and wrap it all up, get things done. So this wasn't something that I was thinking about at the time. It wasn't something that was constantly going on in my mind. I wasn't thinking about where my daughters were, whether they were perhaps doing their homework for the next day in their own rooms or whatever. It all happened very quickly, and there were too many things at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So how long, what period of time elapsed, from the telephone call from your husband until he arrived through the door?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: I can't answer that question. I don't know. I can't be sufficiently specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I'd like you to see. Somewhere between 11 and 12 at night, would that be a fair estimate?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: No. I assume it could have been by 1800 hours, that time of the evening, but I can't be more specific than that, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So if one was talking about it and you are calculating when your husband arrived, you think he was there by about 1800 hours. Would that be a fair way of putting it?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: No, he could not have -- he could not have reached home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Mrs. Mrksic's answer was in relation to the phone call, whether she could remember when she received the phone call, and now her answer is being twisted around to mean something else. She said 1800 hours in relation to the phone call, but Mr. Moore is now using that to imply that's when he arrived, which is simply erroneous, or at least that's how I see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's not altogether clear in the questioning, Mr. Moore, but it was introduced with the phone call. So I think if there's any indication, the 1800 hours does refer to the telephone call. If you want to clarify it, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think -- well, I did ask you the question, what period of time elapsed from the telephone call until your husband arrived through the door, and you said you couldn't answer that. And I said, "Somewhere between 11 and 12 at night, would that be a fair statement?" And you said, "No. I assume it could have been by 1800 hours." Now, I'm just trying to calculate or for you to estimate what the time estimate was from the telephone call until he came through the door.

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: It's very difficult for me to estimate simply because I wasn't watching the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, but this was a special situation. Your husband was coming back after approximately two months. So I would suggest to you just -- not only you, but virtually every husband and wife who haven't seen each other, normally they look forward to seeing each other.

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: I was often alone while he was away elsewhere on some business or other. It was nothing that I wasn't used to. All I wanted is to have him back safe, alive, and well. That's all that counted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I deal -- I will move on to another topic. Often in translation we get variations, and often - and I mean no criticism - it can change. But when you were being asked what day it was, you said the day before St. Andjel's day, which would imply it's on the 20th, and he said he had some commitment. I want to deal with that area of evidence. Can we take it that you don't have a diary?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: No, I don't keep a diary and I don't have an agenda. This happened on the 120th of November. When I said commitments, I meant at the federal secretary the next day. But he didn't say anything when the federal secretary the next day. But he didn't say anything when we spoke on the phone. The commitments, he said, the next day would be in the form of a reception.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I don't know what it's like in the Yugoslav army. Sometimes when you have receptions in other armies, wives go along. Did you go to the reception with your husband, or was it a soldier-only event?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: This was a reception with soldiers only in attendance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what time did he come back on the 21st?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: The 21st, yes, he returned on the evening of the 21st.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What time, approximately?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I was with the sister, and I had to look after her.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I ask you about the sister? When was it she arrived on the 20th? Can you give us an estimate of time when that was?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: Not a very precise estimate. Perhaps an hour later. Perhaps. Perhaps less, as I've previously shared with Counsel Domazet. I think possibly less, but it's very difficult to say and I can't be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But what time did she come, approximately? What time did she come through the door? Not just the interval but the time.

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: Truly, I don't know. I wasn't watching the time. It was an extremely busy day. Everything they were saying on the news, and the news programme was longer than usual, and then both of them arrived. It was a very busy time for me and I wasn't watching the time. There was no time to watch the time. All I know is on the 20th we went to bed earlier than usual. It might have been about 11.00, because I still remember that we had to get up early the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I then summarise it in this way: That you remember your husband arriving because of the news programme; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: That's right, I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And there were numerous news programmes that evening?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: That's right. A lot of coverage, especially Vukovar, all these special programmes devoted to those events. It was particularly pinpointed in that particular programme that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Coric, did Coric come up to the flat with your husband?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: No, no, Coric didn't, he didn't come with my husband.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So, really, the first -- the first thing that came to your attention was your husband's arrival, and he came unaccompanied.

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, he came alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I want to ask you now about the telephone call that your husband apparently made. Is it right to say you didn't hear him make a telephone call; you only found out about that later on?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: I heard him make a phone call. I didn't know who to. I later learned that he was calling the operations centre, the SAC, the military car pool.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So in the translation we have, we've got, "He called somebody but I only found out about this later." That means that you were aware of the phone call but not to whom it was going; is that right? Is that what you're now saying?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't know who he was calling. I wasn't standing there with him to check. I just heard that he have was phoning about an address and asking for a vehicle to be sent over.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The driver who brought Mr. Mrksic's sister was Nenad Relic; is that how you pronounce it?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: That's right. The driver who brought his sister there was Nenad Relic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Had you met or seen that driver before?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: This was the first time I saw him, and this was the only time he ever came to our flat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And so the driver sat down with the commanding officer of the guards division of -- the commander of OG South and shared a glass of wine, did he?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. He drank the glass of wine. He seemed in a hurry and he soon left. I know they shook hands. I went to the bathroom with the sister so I wasn't paying that much attention to what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If you haven't spoken to the lawyers before coming into court, how did you know the name of this driver, if this was the only time you ever met him, 15 years after the event?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: I didn't find out about the name until later, the driver's name I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, who told you about the driver's name, if it wasn't the lawyers?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: Counsel Vasic was the one I asked. I didn't know what the driver's name was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So when did you speak to Counsel Vasic about this name?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: Two days ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So have you been speaking to Counsel Vasic before coming to court?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: He called me to tell me that I should go and testify. The only thing I asked him about this what's his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Why should you ask any questions about the driver's name? It's got nothing to do with you, has it, if you don't know his name?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: I wanted to know the name. Why? Simply because I wanted to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But there was no reason to know, no reason to ask at all. Your evidence was that a driver brought your husband. That's the end of story, isn't it? No need. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. No, rather no. I needed to ask just because this man was in our house, and all these years later I just felt curious. I wanted to know his name because I had forgotten it. And since he was in my home at that one time, I wanted to know his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Have you spoken to any other person about this case, apart from Counsel Vasic?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: I didn't talk to anyone else about the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Do you know Miodrag Panic?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: We don't socialise. I do know him, though. He worked in the guards unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We know that Miodrag Panic is helping Mr. Vasic in some ways. Did you have any conversation at any time with Miodrag Panic?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: I did not have any conversation with Miodrag Panic at any points in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Have you had any dealings with a gentleman called Tesic, Borivoje Tesic?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: His name rings a bell. I think he has a different job now, at least that's what I seem to remember reading in the press. I never met him, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And one final name. Do you know of the name of Vukasinovic?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: What about the first name? Vukasinovic, I don't know. Vukasinovic is not a name I'm familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm told it may well be Ljubisa.

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: Not familiar. Never heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm nearly finished. Can I just go through with two or three other areas. You told us that your husband was involved with the guards for a considerable period of time. Would it be right to say that he was immensely proud of being a guards officer.

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: My husband was with the guards throughout. He's proud of his calling. He was a professional soldier. He was training to become a professional soldier. It wasn't during the war that he became an officer. He was very proud of his job, and he loved his job.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did he ever explain to you that there is a widely held belief that the guards were sent to Vukovar because they had gone to Adzic, who was chief of staff, with an attempt to replace Kadirevic and that he was part of that delegation?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You're aware that he has given evidence in court in Belgrade about the Ovcara massacres or killings. You're aware of that fact, I presume?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: A court in Belgrade? I don't remember. It's possible, however, that he has given evidence in some court, rather, but I don't remember when.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did he ever tell you, from your recollection, that he's given statements or evidence, I think, in two courts- one in Belgrade and I think one in Novi Sad? Did he ever tell you that?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: He never told me about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Are you aware that various suggestions and allegations have also been made against him about his behaviour in Bosnia? Did you ever hear that allegation?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear that. There are courts, and it is their job to establish whether it's true or not. I never heard that my husband did anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. Let us, then, conclude in the following way: On the morning of the 22nd, your husband left the flat; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the 22nd of November, my husband left the apartment early in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And can you give us an indication of what time he left?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: He left early in the morning. Another sister and her husband went as well. She had come to see the other sister. And I know that we all had coffee together in the morning. I remember that it was very early. It could have been before 7. And this sister and her family also left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: MR. MOORE: I'm going to ask to go into private session, if I may, for the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We're nearly at the time of our --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I've nearly finished, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I want to go back to the 20th/21st. You say that your husband went off in the morning of the 21st. He was collected by a driver. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: The driver didn't come up. He just rang the intercom bell downstairs, and he went with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And on the 22nd?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: On the 22nd, he didn't leave with the driver. The same driver waited downstairs in the car in front of the building. My daughter Jelena was on her way to school near Kalinic market, and she asked the driver, "Are you waiting for my father, Mr. Mrksic?" And the driver said, "Yes, that's right." And she said my father had already left. And he asked where she was going, and she said she was on her way to school, and so the driver offered to take her there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: On the 22nd, did you see an officer called Tesic?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: Nobody came to the apartment that morning. No, I didn't see anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would suggest to you that almost certainly you are wrong, that your husband did not come that night but came the following morning and only stayed one night with you, not two. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: I do understand. He came on the 20th, in the evening. We were all together, the sister and the family.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Where did the sister sleep that night? Because I think you have a three-bedroom flat; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct. The sister slept in the small room, and my daughter, who normally use that is room, I moved her to a sofa chair in her sister's room. And the bed remained all made up, because I thought that the sister would come back. But after she went to the bus station, she didn't come back, even though I was expecting her to return.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, would a break now be convenient?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, even though I have only one or two questions. So if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, we're nearly at the end of the tape, so I think we should break now and that will give you time to reflect over your questions, and I think it might help Mrs. Mrksic to have a little break now. We will resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Mrksic, towards the end of the last session, you said in reply to Mr. Moore's question something about where the sister slept. You gave us some details and you said that you left the bed all made up for her, expecting her to return. It wasn't quite clear. So would you please tell us now, when were you expecting her to return?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: She was supposed to go with her friend Anka to look for her husband, so she left. And she was also supposed to meet the children. I was expecting her to come back. But the family was looking for each other, they were in the process of finding each other, and there was no need for her to come back to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: All right. So when you accompanied her to this place, when was it?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: It was on Tuesday. She came on Thursday, when the Guards Brigade returned, on the 24th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: That's a bit more clear. So that's what you had in mind. There was another question dealing with what your husband did on the 21st, namely, that in the morning he left the apartment and came back in the evening. That's what you said. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. He left in the morning and he came back in the evening hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did he tell you about what he had done that day?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't tell me anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Another question. You had a lot of questions about what you discussed with him. Most of these questions focused on the Vukovar events. I want to ask you this: Given the long career of your husband, and you were married to him throughout that time, was it usual for him to tell you about his works, things that he did at work, his colleagues, and so on? Did he typically discuss that with you before this period and after this period, in general, throughout his career?

utterances.speaker: DJUDJICA MRKSIC
utterances.text: In general, he never talked about his job. He never talked about his colleagues or anything job-related.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have concluded my redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Domazet. Mrs. Mrksic, I am pleased to be able to tell you that that completes the questioning of you. The Chamber is grateful that you were able to come here at, it seems, quite short notice and for the assistance you've been able to give us. You are free now to leave whenever it's convenient to return, but that's not suggesting that you must leave now. You may want to remain here a little while.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, what is the position about the next available witness? Could we ask?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, given that we spoke about this on Monday, and that at the time I was told that it would be very difficult to ensure the presence of the witness who was subpoenaed so as to be here and testify for three days this week, I worked with Mr. Vasic to ensure the presence of today's witness, Mrs. Mrksic. In the meantime, we were told that all preparations were completed for the arrival of our witness tomorrow, Bisic Stevan, who is scheduled to arrive in the afternoon and he will be able to testify only on Friday. So unfortunately we don't have a witness available for tomorrow due to these circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, do you want to commence your case as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to say something that has to do with our Defence case, and I think it will be useful for everyone if I were to address the Chamber now with our request. I assume that we are done for the day, so before we leave the courtroom, let me tell you this: This partially stems from Mr. Moore's question today in cross-examination and has to do with a procedural issue that both Mr. Borovic and I wanted to raise, and I think it will be of interest to the third Defence team as well, perhaps later on; namely, you are aware that in the pre-trial brief and in the documents proposed at the time by the OTP in their 65 ter list of exhibits they planned to introduce, there were also documents or, rather, statements given by our clients before various judicial organs in our country. You were able to see on the 65 ter list three statements of all three clients taken by the security administration in 1998, and then there were three statements that they gave as witnesses before the military court in the proceedings that you are familiar with, that you learned of during the Prosecution case. Towards the end of the Prosecution case, Mr. Moore first announced that he wanted to introduce those statements into evidence, and then you gave us a deadline to respond to that request. And then Mr. Moore informed the Chamber orally that they were not going to tender that into evidence, but then asked that he be allowed to use those statements in cross-examination should our clients decide to testify. Since today Mr. Moore put several questions related to the content of the statement of Mr. Mrksic, and since Mr. Theunens, in his evidence, also referred to some facts from those statements, we would like to advance some arguments showing that these statements are absolutely inappropriate, both when analysed in light of the Rules of this Tribunal as well as in light of the provisions of the then valid Yugoslav criminal and criminal/procedural law. They are absolutely unfit to be used in court. But since Mr. Moore gave up on his initial request, we decided to postpone this motion. This was not a factor in deciding whether our clients are going to testify or not. But now, since this involves serious arguments that we would like to present to you, and we would like to do it in writing, would you please give us an eight-day deadline in which we can explain why we believe that these statements may not be tendered into evidence or used in cross-examination so that, following that, you could rule on whether Mr. Moore is allowed to use them in cross-examination when our clients start testifying. We would like to give you written arguments as to why we believe that these statements are inadmissible. This false under Rule 89(D), because we think that this goes against the interests of justice. This is my submission. We would like for you to set a deadline for us to submit this in writing, and if not, then we would ask that we present our arguments orally. But, once again, we need sufficient notice in order to prepare ourselves. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I take it, Mr. Borovic, that's effectively a joint submission of yourself and Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honours. We were just wondering whether I need to clarify this further. But if this is sufficient, then we would like to submit a written motion on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're of the mind that you should have the time you seek, eight days, within which to file any submissions you wish to make and to serve them on the other parties. The Prosecution would have a week to respond to that, if necessary. And if Mr. Domazet wants to add anything, he certainly would have leave to do so. Not now but in the written submissions. So after service, within eight days, Mr. Domazet and Mr. Moore will have a further week within which they may wish to put something. That being so, we must now adjourn. We're not making any comment on the circumstances that have arisen, but we will be looking at the question of witnesses in the three cases, next week as foreshadowed. We will -- oh, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry, I didn't mean to interrupt. It's quite simply one matter that I know there's going to be a ruling -- well, I suspect there will be a ruling. The Court had made an order that there should be appropriate summaries by this Friday in relation to the witnesses principally from the defence of Mr. Mrksic. I've spoken to my learned friend, Mr. Domazet. For him to answer now, if the Court wishes, but the impression I get is we will not have appropriate summaries. If that is the case, we would submit that that is unfair. We have done everything we can to accommodate Mr. Mrksic's predicament, but we are now finding ourselves wholly disadvantaged by not having summaries of any consequence at all. The Court has made, I think, many lenient orders, and I don't mean that unkindly, because of the circumstances. But the time has now come, we would submit, where we must have proper summaries in accordance with the Rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: As I recall it, there are five witnesses in respect of whom the order is for this Friday and the balance later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Perhaps Mr. Domazet can assist the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That is the order, and at the moment we proceed on the basis that it is going to be complied with, unless Mr. Domazet is going to stand now and say that it won't be.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we will definitely abide by the ruling. I will do my best to even do it before the deadline, if possible. If I can remember, our deadline is by Friday. And for the next group of witnesses, the first five are already available with summaries, and I think that we need to give summaries for witnesses 6 to 10. If possible, we will do even summaries beyond those first 10. And then, as I said to you, Mr. Vasic will be available next week, and as soon as he's here, he and I will go over the witness list and we will try to shorten it and -- in relation to the witnesses who will be withdrawn, we will not be providing summaries for them. But at any rate, we will comply with the ruling. I don't want Mr. Moore to have any concerns about us not meeting deadlines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Domazet. I think the matter must lie there, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In the circumstances, we must now adjourn until Friday morning, at 9. And on Friday morning, we're in Courtroom III, just so that people turn up in the right courtroom. We will now adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 1st day of September, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.16 p.m.,
